22.title: Before anything, a voice (Genesis 1:1–5)
22.hook: the Torah opens "in the beginning" and speaks light into the dark
22.howItsDone: Jews read Bereshit as the first weekly Torah portion each autumn, right after Simchat Torah, and the first chapter of Genesis is one of the most studied passages in Jewish learning.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the parsha, the weekly portion, and camp one's twenty-one words. Your line was join the cycle wherever it is. Today, we step in at the very start. Day twenty-two.

Welcome to camp two: the stories. The original serial, told one episode at a time, the way a whole people has told it for thousands of years. And every serial needs an opening scene. Here it is. There's no light. No ground. No sky. The text calls it unformed and void, darkness over the deep, and a wind, or a spirit, hovering over the water. Nothing has happened yet. Nobody is there to see it. And then, before any thing, before a single star, there's a sound. Someone speaks. Today: the first word of the Torah, and the first words spoken in it.
screen: `CAMP TWO: THE STORIES.` → `DARKNESS OVER THE DEEP.` → `THEN, A VOICE.`

segments.voice: The Torah's first word is Bereshit. In the beginning. It's also the Hebrew name of the whole book of Genesis, and of the first weekly portion. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Even that first word is argued over. The great medieval commentator Rashi pointed out that the Hebrew grammar reads more like "in the beginning of God's creating," as if the verse is setting a scene rather than announcing the very first moment. Scholars still debate it. And the rabbis noticed the first letter, bet, which looks like a box closed on three sides and open only toward the front, the direction the Hebrew is read. One midrash says: that's a hint. What came before, what's above and below, isn't for you to chase. Start from here, and go forward. Then the first thing God does in the story isn't to build or to shape. It's to speak. "And God said: 'Let there be light.' And there was light." A sentence, and the world answers it. The Mishnah says the world was created with ten sayings, ten times "and God said." And the first day closes, "And there was evening and there was morning, one day." Not the first day. One day, as if there's nothing yet to count against. Why does this matter on an ordinary Tuesday? Because the Torah starts with the idea that words make things. The book of Proverbs puts it bluntly: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue." A sentence at breakfast can make or wreck a whole day for someone.
screen: `BERESHIT — IN THE BEGINNING.` · `BET: CLOSED BEHIND, OPEN AHEAD.` · `LET THERE BE LIGHT.` · `TEN SAYINGS MADE THE WORLD.` · then, large: `DEATH AND LIFE ARE IN THE POWER OF THE TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, with the bell. Sit, and let it be dark for a moment: close your eyes. Then think of one person you'll talk to today. Choose one kind sentence you could say to them, a true one, specific, not a compliment you'd give anybody. Turn it over until it's exactly right. When you open your eyes, you'll have it ready. The bell holds the time.
Bereshit. In the beginning: the Torah's first word, where God speaks, and light answers.
Your line: words make worlds. Before noon today, say that kind sentence out loud, to the person you chose. Watch what it makes. Day twenty-two.

23.title: Six days of making (Genesis 1:6–31)
23.hook: sky, sea, land, lights, creatures, each day closing "and it was good"
23.howItsDone: Jews read the six days of creation in the first Torah portion each autumn, and in the daily morning prayers praise God who renews the work of creation every day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Bereshit. In the beginning, a voice, and light answered. Your line was words make worlds. Did your kind sentence get said? Day twenty-three.

Think about moving into an empty apartment. First you need the rooms: walls, a floor, a window that lets the light in. Only then do you bring in what fills them: a lamp for the corner, fish in a tank, a cat on the windowsill, people around a table. Nobody hangs a picture before there's a wall. Back on day six you met the refrain of the first chapter, and it was good. Today we walk through the days themselves, sky, sea, land, lights and creatures, and notice that the chapter is built a lot like that apartment.
screen: `AN EMPTY APARTMENT.` → `FIRST THE ROOMS.` → `THEN WHAT FILLS THEM.`

segments.voice: Here are the six days. One: light, separated from dark. Two: a dome of sky, separating the waters above from the waters below. Three: dry land appears, and plants grow on it. Four: the sun, the moon and the stars. Five: fish in the sea and birds in the sky. Six: animals on the land, and then human beings. Readers, from medieval commentators to modern scholars, have noticed the pattern. The first three days make spaces: day, sky and sea, land. The next three fill them, in the same order: lights for the day, fish and birds for the sea and sky, creatures for the land. Rooms, then furniture. Now a puzzle the rabbis loved. There's light on day one, but no sun until day four. So what was that first light? The Talmud says it was a special light, by which a person could see from one end of the world to the other, and God hid it away for the righteous in the time to come. Some modern readers see something else in the order: the sun and moon, which many ancient peoples worshiped, show up here as lamps, made on a Wednesday, doing a job. And the word for day, yom? Jewish readers have long disagreed about whether these are days of twenty-four hours, and the chapter doesn't stop to say. What it does say, over and over, is that each thing is made "after its kind," each creature fully itself. And at the end of the sixth day, looking at all of it together: "and, behold, it was very good." Six days of making, and the chapter keeps count of the good.
screen: `THREE DAYS OF ROOMS.` · `THREE DAYS TO FILL THEM.` · `LIGHT BEFORE THE SUN.` · `EACH AFTER ITS KIND.` · then, large: `AND, BEHOLD, IT WAS VERY GOOD.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, with the bell. Open your eyes and look around, slowly, and name six good things you can see, one for each day. Something with light in it. Something from the sky, even just the air or a window. Something that grew. Something that shines. Something alive. And a person, or a trace of one: a photo, a handwritten note, your own hands. Say each one quietly, then let the list sit. The bell holds the time.
Six days of making. Three days of rooms, three days of filling them, and the good counted all the way through.
Your line: count the good. Tonight, before bed, count six good things from today, out loud or on your fingers, one for each day of making. Day twenty-three.

24.title: In the image (Genesis 1:26–27)
24.hook: every person is made in God's image; the rabbis say a king's coins look alike, but God's people never do (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5)
24.howItsDone: Jewish teaching and law draw on tzelem Elohim for the dignity of every person, from the care of the sick to the honor given to the dead; the Mishnah's saying about saving one life as saving a whole world is widely quoted.

segments.voice: Yesterday: six days of making, rooms first, then what fills them. Your line was count the good. Did you get to six? Day twenty-four.
screen: `SIX DAYS OF MAKING — COUNT THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Take a coin out of your pocket, or picture one. There's a face on it, a president or a queen. Now take out another coin of the same kind. Same face. Exactly the same, down to the last line of the hair. That's the whole point of a coin: every one stamped from the same die, identical, interchangeable. You don't care which quarter you get. Now look around at the next ten people you see today. Not one of them is the same. Nearly two thousand years ago, the rabbis looked at those two facts side by side, and made them into one of the boldest teachings in Jewish law. Today: the image.
screen: `TWO COINS, THE SAME FACE.` → `TEN PEOPLE, NO TWO ALIKE.` → `THE RABBIS PUT THEM TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: On the sixth day, the Torah slows down. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And God created man in His own image, in the image of God created He him; male and female created He them." In Hebrew: tzelem Elohim. Tzelem is an image, a likeness, the word used for a statue or a figure. Elohim is God. Every human being, the verse says, carries God's likeness. What that likeness is, the Torah doesn't explain. Maimonides said it's the mind, the ability to understand. Others say it's freedom, the power to choose, or the power to create, or to love. The text leaves the question open. Now the coins. The Mishnah, describing how judges warned witnesses in a capital case, says this. A human king stamps many coins with one seal, and they all look alike. But the King of kings stamped every person with the seal of the first human, and not one of them is like another. God's image makes us different, not the same. And from there the Mishnah goes further. Why was humanity created from a single person? So that whoever destroys one life is as if they destroyed a whole world, and whoever saves one life is as if they saved a whole world. And so no one can say to anyone else, my ancestor was greater than yours. And so each person is obliged to say: the world was created for my sake. Two rabbis once argued over the greatest principle in the Torah. Rabbi Akiva said: love your neighbor as yourself. Ben Azzai pointed to the verse about humanity made in God's likeness, and said his was greater, because it covers everyone.
screen: `TZELEM ELOHIM — THE IMAGE OF GOD.` · `WHAT IS THE IMAGE? IT DOESN'T SAY.` · `ONE SEAL, NO TWO ALIKE.` · `ONE LIFE IS A WHOLE WORLD.` · then, large: `IN THE IMAGE OF GOD CREATED HE HIM.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, with the bell. Bring to mind the face of someone you passed today and barely noticed: a cashier, a driver, someone on the street. Try to see them clearly. The shape of the face. The expression. The one detail that makes it theirs and nobody else's. If you believe what the verse says, hold that face as carrying God's image. If you don't, hold it as one entire world. The bell holds the time.
Tzelem Elohim. The image of God, stamped on every person, so that no two are alike.
Your line: no two faces alike. Today, look at one stranger's face with care, long enough to remember one thing that is only theirs. Day twenty-four.

25.title: The seventh day (Genesis 2:1–3)
25.hook: God finishes, then stops, and blesses the stopping itself
25.howItsDone: On Friday night, many Jews recite Genesis 2:1–3, beginning with the word vayechulu, at the start of kiddush over wine, closing the week with the story of the seventh day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tzelem Elohim, the image of God, one seal and no two faces alike. Your line was no two faces alike. Whose face did you really see? Day twenty-five.

It's Friday night in a Jewish home. The candles are lit. The table is set. Someone stands and lifts a full cup of wine, and before any blessing over it, they recite a few lines from Genesis. Three verses, the ones right after the six days of making. Every Friday night, all over the world, the week is closed with the same words. You met the Sabbath back on day three, and its commandment on day seven. Today, we go to where it starts in the story: the day God stopped, and did something to the stopping.
screen: `FRIDAY NIGHT. A FULL CUP.` → `THREE VERSES FROM GENESIS.` → `THE DAY GOD STOPPED.`

segments.voice: The heaven and the earth are finished, the story says, and all their host. Then, in the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And on the seventh day God finished His work which He had made." Wait. Finished on the seventh day? Wasn't the work done on the sixth? The rabbis noticed. Rashi, quoting an older midrash, gives a beautiful answer. After six days the world had everything, except one thing. It was missing rest. Menuchah. So on the seventh day, rest was created, and with rest, the work was finally complete. A world without stopping wasn't finished yet. Then comes the line: "And God blessed the seventh day, and hallowed it." Hallowed means made holy. In Hebrew it's the first time anything in the whole Torah is called holy, and what's called holy isn't a mountain, or a temple, or a person. It's a day. A stretch of time. The twentieth-century rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel built a whole book around that detail. And one more thing readers have noticed. Every other day of creation closes with "there was evening and there was morning." The seventh day doesn't. The refrain never comes. Some readers take that as a hint that the rest the seventh day started is still open, and hasn't ended. The text doesn't explain it. It just leaves the day open. So the story ends not with a final product but with a pause, and the pause is the part that's blessed. Finished isn't when the last thing is made. Finished is when you stop.
screen: `FINISHED ON THE SEVENTH DAY?` · `THE MISSING PIECE WAS REST.` · `THE FIRST HOLY THING IS A DAY.` · `NO EVENING, NO MORNING.` · then, large: `AND GOD BLESSED THE SEVENTH DAY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, with the bell, and today the practice is simply to stop. Put down whatever is in your hands. Don't plan, don't tidy your thoughts, don't try to relax properly. If a task comes to mind, let it wait outside the door. Nothing needs to be made in this minute for it to be complete. If you pray, you can let the stopping itself be the prayer. The bell holds the time.
The seventh day. The day God stopped, and blessed the stopping, and called a stretch of time holy.
Your line: finished is holy. Today, when you finish one thing, don't reach straight for the next. Stop for sixty seconds, and let it be done. Day twenty-five.

26.title: Dust and breath (Genesis 2:4–7)
26.hook: the first human is shaped from adamah, the earth, and given breath
26.howItsDone: Jews read the second creation story in the first Torah portion each autumn; each morning's prayers begin by thanking God for returning the soul, the neshamah, and the Hasidic teaching of the two pockets is often retold.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the seventh day, when rest finished the world. Your line was finished is holy. Did you stop for sixty seconds after something was done? Day twenty-six.

Picture a potter at a wheel, or a kid at the beach, hands wet, shaping something out of mud. It's close work. Thumbs pressing, fingers smoothing, the maker bent right over the thing being made. In the first chapter of Genesis, God makes the world from far away, by speaking: let there be. In the second chapter the camera comes down close. The story starts again, and this time God kneels in the dirt, and shapes a person with, as it were, bare hands. Then leans in closer still. Today: dust, and breath, and the name of the first human.
screen: `A POTTER, HANDS IN THE CLAY.` → `THE STORY STARTS AGAIN, CLOSE UP.` → `DUST, THEN BREATH.`

segments.voice: In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "Then the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Listen to the Hebrew underneath. The ground is adamah. The human made from it is adam. Adam isn't only a name at first. It's a word: the earthling, the one from the earth. Human, from humus, soil, is almost the same pun in English. And formed is the word for what a potter does. Then the breath. God breathes into the nostrils, face to face, the breath of life, nishmat chayim. The Hebrew for breath, neshamah, is the same word Jews use for the soul. So the soul, in this picture, is a breath that came from very close. The rabbis added a detail: the dust for the first human was gathered from every corner of the earth, so that no place could say, the first human came from here, and not from you. Every land is home. And a Hasidic teacher, Rabbi Simcha Bunim of Peshischa, told his students to carry two slips of paper, one in each pocket. On one: for my sake the world was created, from the Mishnah we met on day twenty-four. On the other: I am but dust and ashes, Abraham's words to God on day eight. When you feel too proud, reach for the dust. When you feel worthless, reach for the other pocket. The trick, he said, is knowing which pocket to reach into. Earth and breath. Both are true of you, all the time.
screen: `ADAMAH — THE GROUND. ADAM — THE EARTHLING.` · `NESHAMAH — BREATH, AND SOUL.` · `DUST FROM EVERY CORNER.` · `TWO POCKETS.` · then, large: `AND MAN BECAME A LIVING SOUL.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, with the bell. Put both feet flat on the floor and feel them there, pressing down toward the ground you're made of. Then breathe in slowly through your nose, and notice the air coming in close, the way the story says the first breath did. Feet: earth. Nose: breath. Stay with both, back and forth. The bell holds the time.
Adam. The earthling, shaped from adamah, the ground, and given breath from very close.
Your line: earth and breath. Today, when you feel too big or too small, remember the two pockets, and reach into the one you need. Day twenty-six.

27.title: Not good to be alone (Genesis 2:18–25)
27.hook: the first thing the Torah calls "not good" is loneliness
27.howItsDone: Jewish tradition treats companionship as a basic need: study is often done in pairs, called chavruta, many prayers are said in community, and visiting the lonely and the sick is counted a mitzvah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: adam, the earthling, shaped from dust and given breath. Your line was earth and breath. Which pocket did you reach into? Day twenty-seven.

So far, everything in this story has been good. Light, good. Land, good. Sun and moon, fish and birds, good. At the end of the sixth day, very good. Seven times we heard it, back on day six. Then, in the second chapter, there's the human, alone in the garden. Plenty to eat. Nothing dangerous. Nothing wrong at all, you'd think. And for the first time in the whole Torah, God looks at something and says it's not good. Not a sin. Not a monster. Not a flood. Something you might feel on a Sunday afternoon with your phone in your hand. Today: the first not good.
screen: `GOOD, GOOD, VERY GOOD.` → `A HUMAN, ALONE IN A GARDEN.` → `THE FIRST NOT GOOD.`

segments.voice: In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him a help meet for him." The first not good is loneliness. Now, that old phrase, help meet. It gave English the word helpmate, and it's often heard as a helper, an assistant. The Hebrew is ezer kenegdo. Ezer means help, but in the Bible that word is used most often of God. The Psalms say, in the same translation, "My help cometh from the LORD." That's ezer. It's not a junior word. And kenegdo means opposite him, facing him, alongside him as an equal. Someone who can look you in the eye. Rashi noticed that kenegdo can also mean against him, and he gave a wry answer: if you're worthy, a help; if not, someone who pushes back. Anyone who's been in a close relationship recognizes both. Then, in the story, the animals come. The human names each one, and none of them is the one. Something is still missing. The human sleeps, and a second person is made from the first, from the side, the text says. And the first human speaks the Torah's first human words, almost a song: "This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh." At last. The rabbis extended the idea far beyond marriage. There's a story in the Talmud about Honi, a man who slept for seventy years, woke up, and found that nobody knew him anymore. His conclusion became a proverb: either companionship, or death. Friendship, study partners, community, family. People need people, and the Torah says it right at the start, before anything else goes wrong.
screen: `THE FIRST NOT GOOD: ALONE.` · `EZER — THE WORD USED FOR GOD.` · `KENEGDO — FACING, AS AN EQUAL.` · `BONE OF MY BONES.` · then, large: `EITHER COMPANIONSHIP, OR DEATH.`

segments.voice: Two minutes, with the bell. Think of someone who might be lonely right now. An older neighbor. A friend who moved away. A coworker who eats lunch by themselves. Someone who went quiet in the group chat. Picture their face. Then decide exactly what you'll send them: not a long message, just a real one. Hold it until the bell ends. The bell holds the time.
Not good to be alone. The first thing in the Torah called not good, and the help that faces you as an equal.

28.title: The garden and the question (Genesis 3)
28.hook: the fruit, the hiding, and God's first question to a person: "Where art thou?"
28.howItsDone: Jews read the garden story in the first Torah portion each autumn; the question ayekah, where are you, is a favorite theme of sermons and Hasidic teaching as a call to honest self-examination.

segments.voice: Yesterday: not good to be alone, the first not good in the Torah. Your line was not good alone. Did your message reach someone? Day twenty-eight, the end of week four.

Every parent knows this moment. It's quiet. Too quiet. You walk into the room, and there's a small child behind the couch, very still, with chocolate on their face. You know exactly what happened. They know you know. And still you ask: where are you? In the garden, there's one tree whose fruit the two humans were told not to eat. A snake starts a conversation. They eat. Their eyes are opened, they see they're naked, and they sew fig leaves together. Then, in the cool of the day, they hear God walking in the garden, and they hide. Today: the hiding, and the question.

segments.voice: First, a myth to clear up. It wasn't an apple. The text just says fruit. The rabbis guessed: some said a fig, since fig leaves were right there; others said grapes, or wheat, or a citron. The apple came much later, in European art. Now the moment everything turns on. In the Jewish Publication Society's 1917 translation: "And the LORD God called unto the man, and said unto him: 'Where art thou?'" In Hebrew, one word: ayekah. It's the first question God asks a human being in the Torah. And it's strange, because God obviously knows where he is. So why ask? The answer many Jewish teachers give is that the question isn't for God. It's for the man. It's an opening, a door left ajar: come out and say where you are. And what does the man do with the door? He answers, and then he points: the woman you gave me, she gave me the fruit. And the woman points at the snake. The first question, and the first blame, passed along like a hot plate. There's a famous Hasidic story. The founder of Chabad, Rabbi Shneur Zalman of Liadi, was in a Russian prison, and a jailer asked him mockingly: if God knows everything, why ask Adam where he was? The rabbi answered: in every age, God calls to every person: where are you in your world? So many years of your life have passed. Where are you? This week you met Bereshit, the six days of making, tzelem Elohim, the seventh day, adam, not good to be alone, and now the first question. It still hangs in the air.

segments.voice: Two minutes, with the bell. Let the question land on you, not as an accusation, but as a door left open: where are you? Not your location. Where are you in your life right now? What are you hiding behind, if anything? What would it take to step out from behind the tree? You don't have to answer out loud. Just answer honestly. The bell holds the time.
The garden and the question. The fruit, the hiding, and God's first question to a person: where are you?
